sourceHtml:
An AI agent that updates a ticket or reads a customer record acts for a person, inside applications that person can reach. Your identity team then has to answer a question that per-app OAuth consent and shared service accounts leave open: which agent might act for which user in which application, and how you stop it. Okta Cross App Access (XAA) answers it in your identity provider (IdP). You register the agent in Okta, an administrator approves the applications it might reach, and Okta evaluates policy each time the agent asks to act for a user. In our tests, after an administrator removed a user’s assignment to the agent, Okta refused the agent’s new requests for that user within about 1 second, and tokens already issued expired within 5 minutes.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This solution uses two of its capabilities to carry out Okta’s decision on AWS. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, validates Okta’s grant. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeems it for a short-lived access token with credentials your agent code doesn’t see, and keeps that token in its token vault. In our tests, AgentCore Identity added about 0.6 seconds to a request that took about 30 seconds end to end.

In this post, the first of two, you build a task agent on AgentCore runtime that acts for signed-in users through XAA and AgentCore Identity. You configure the AgentCore Identity parts it needs, enforce each user’s authority in the tools, and see what we measured: what each check refuses, the practices we settled on, and how fast Okta’s controls take effect. Part 2 then puts the same governance behind Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Cedar policies, a second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), and an audit trail in Amazon CloudWatch.

Solution overview

Okta is the governance plane: it decides which agent might act for which user, against which resource. AgentCore Identity is the execution plane: it holds the agent’s credentials, turns Okta’s decision into a token the resource accepts, and keeps both identities in that token. In Figure 1, the agent and the two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers it calls all run on AgentCore runtime.

Figure 1: Solution architecture, with numbers matching the steps that follow

Each request carries three tokens, and each records a different decision: the ID token says who the user is, the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) is Okta’s decision, and the access token is what the resource accepts. One request flows like this:

  1. The user signs in to the web front end, a backend for frontend (BFF), with OpenID Connect through the agent’s linked Okta app.
  2. For each request, the BFF exchanges the user’s ID token for an ID-JAG at Okta’s org authorization server, authenticated as the agent (RFC 8693 token exchange). Okta checks that the agent is active, that the user is assigned to it, and that an administrator connected it to the target authorization server for the requested scopes. The ID-JAG is single-use and expires in 5 minutes.
  3. The BFF invokes the agent on AgentCore runtime with the ID-JAG as its bearer token. The runtime’s JWT authorizer accepts only ID-JAGs that Okta issued to this agent.
  4. The runtime gets a workload access token from AgentCore Identity that binds the agent’s workload identity to the user, and passes it to the agent code. This workload access token is an AWS-internal binding token: neither Okta nor the resource sees it, so it isn’t one of the three tokens.
  5. The agent asks AgentCore Identity for an access token. AgentCore Identity redeems the ID-JAG at the resource’s Okta custom authorization server with the JWT authorization grant (RFC 7523), authenticated as the agent. Okta returns a 5-minute access token that names both the user and the agent and carries the user’s groups.
  6. The agent calls the MCP servers with that token. The task manager checks that a registered agent obtained it, and that the user’s group and scope allow the tool.

Figure 2 shows the same request as a sequence, with the check that each party makes.

Figure 2: The three-token chain and the check each party makes, with the step 4 workload access token staying inside AWS

Prerequisites

To follow along, you need the following:

Prerequisite What we used
An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and an Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock US West (Oregon)
An Okta org with Cross App Access for AI agents and API Access Management (custom authorization servers) An Okta Integrator Free Plan org
Python, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), boto3, the AgentCore CLI, and the AgentCore Python SDK, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Python 3.11, AWS CLI version 2, boto3 1.43, AgentCore CLI 0.31.1, and AgentCore Python SDK 1.24.1
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions Permission to create AgentCore resources and IAM roles

The walkthrough takes about 1 hour. AgentCore charges for what you use. See Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing.

The base for this solution is the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain in the AgentCore samples repository on GitHub, and you can build the solution in this post on top of it. Beyond that sample, the snippets and configurations in this post show the pattern conceptually. They aren’t a complete, deployable solution. The code is sample code for non-production use, so work with your security and legal teams to meet your organization’s security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before you deploy it.

Register the agent in Okta

Okta needs an authorization server for the resource, the agent, a connection between them, and a policy that admits the agent’s grant. Do all of these steps in the Okta Admin Console: registering the agent creates its linked app, so you don’t need an app integration wizard.

  1. Create a custom authorization server for the resource application with the audience api://task-manager and the custom scopes xaa:read and xaa:write. Request only the resource’s custom scopes: Okta rejects an ID-JAG request that includes OpenID Connect scopes such as openid or profile (invalid_scope), so a request needs at least one custom scope and no OpenID Connect scopes.
  2. Add a groups claim to its access tokens, filtered to groups that start with xaa-. This claim carries each user’s authority to the tools.
  3. In the Admin Console, go to Directory > AI Agents, choose Register AI agent and then Register manually, optionally assign an owner, and create a linked OpenID Connect app. On Client registration, choose Client secret, generate a secret, and then activate the agent. The agent and the app share one client ID, and that app must sign your users in: an ID token from another app fails the exchange with “the client application is not registered for delegation to this agent.”
  4. On the agent’s Resource connections tab, connect it to the authorization server, limited to the scopes it needs, as Figure 3 shows.
  5. Add an access policy rule to the custom authorization server that allows the agent’s JWT Bearer grant, with a 5-minute access token lifetime. Without the grant type, the second exchange fails with no_matching_policy, and the lifetime bounds how long a revoked delegation keeps working.
  6. Assign the users or groups who might act through the agent. They sign in through the linked app, so give it an app sign-in policy that admits them with the authenticators they’ve enrolled. In our sandbox org, the linked app had its own policy with a rule for the test group. For real users, apply your organization’s policy, including multifactor authentication.

Figure 3: The task agent’s resource connection in Okta, limited to the xaa:read and xaa:write scopes

Okta’s Cross App Access guide covers the console steps, and the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain scripts the authorization server and its JWT bearer policy. The BFF then requests the ID-JAG, authenticated as the agent:

POST /oauth2/v1/token HTTP/1.1
Host: YOUR-ORG.okta.com
Authorization: Basic <the agent's client ID and secret>
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange
&requested_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id-jag
&subject_token=<the user's ID token>
&subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id_token
&audience=https://YOUR-ORG.okta.com/oauth2/YOUR-CUSTOM-AS-ID
&scope=xaa:read xaa:write

The AWS sample 06-okta-xaa sends the same request in Python (agent/xaa_client.py). The BFF authenticates as the agent, so store the agent’s client secret in AWS Secrets Manager rather than in code or configuration files.

Set up AgentCore Identity

AgentCore Identity holds three things for this solution, and your agent code doesn’t see the client secret or call Okta’s token endpoint:

Part of AgentCore Identity What it holds Who creates it
Workload identity The agent’s identity on AWS, bound to the signed-in user for each request AgentCore runtime, for each agent runtime
OAuth2 credential provider The agent’s Okta client ID and secret, and the grant to use You, once per Okta agent
Token vault The access tokens the provider obtains AgentCore Identity

Create the credential provider

The credential provider performs the second exchange. Point it at the custom authorization server, authenticate it as the AI agent, and set the on-behalf-of grant to JWT_AUTHORIZATION_GRANT, which AgentCore Identity sends as jwt-bearer with the ID-JAG as the assertion:

control = boto3.client("bedrock-agentcore-control")
provider = control.create_oauth2_credential_provider(
    name="okta-xaa-obo",
    credentialProviderVendor="CustomOauth2",
    oauth2ProviderConfigInput={"customOauth2ProviderConfig": {
        "oauthDiscovery": {"discoveryUrl": f"{OKTA_ORG}/oauth2/{CUSTOM_AS_ID}/.well-known/openid-configuration"},
        "clientId": AGENT_CLIENT_ID,          # the AI agent's Okta client ID
        "clientSecret": AGENT_CLIENT_SECRET,  # AgentCore Identity stores it in AWS Secrets Manager
        "clientAuthenticationMethod": "CLIENT_SECRET_BASIC",
        "onBehalfOfTokenExchangeConfig": {"grantType": "JWT_AUTHORIZATION_GRANT"},
    }},
)
provider_arn = provider["credentialProviderArn"]

Okta binds both exchanges to the client named in the ID-JAG, so each Okta agent needs its own provider: when we redeemed one agent’s ID-JAG as another, Okta refused with “The ‘client_id’ in the JWT Bearer Grant must match the ‘client_id’ used to authenticate the client.” AgentCore Identity keeps the secret in a service-managed AWS Secrets Manager secret, which you rotate with update-oauth2-credential-provider. If your team already manages the client secret in Secrets Manager, you can reference that secret’s ARN instead. AgentCore Identity reads the client secret from it, so you can rotate the secret without updating the provider (see Reference your own AWS Secrets Manager secrets in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity). To avoid a shared secret, authenticate with a private key instead. See Authenticate with Private Key JWT using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity. Figure 4 shows the provider in the AgentCore console.

Figure 4: The credential provider authenticating as the agent with the JWT authorization grant

Use the workload identity that AgentCore runtime manages

AgentCore runtime creates and manages a workload identity for each agent runtime. When a request passes the runtime’s JWT authorizer, the runtime gets a workload access token for that workload identity and the inbound token’s issuer and subject, and passes it to your code. AgentCore Identity then uses the ID-JAG behind it as the assertion for the exchange.

The AgentCore Python SDK keeps the workload access token in BedrockAgentCoreContext, not in the request headers that your entrypoint receives. Our first version looked for it in the headers, found nothing, and fell back to its own GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT call with a second workload identity, on all 21 requests we checked. Read it from the context instead:

from bedrock_agentcore.runtime import BedrockAgentCoreContext

identity = boto3.client("bedrock-agentcore")

def okta_access_token() -> str:
    workload_token = BedrockAgentCoreContext.get_workload_access_token()  # minted by the runtime
    return identity.get_resource_oauth2_token(
        workloadIdentityToken=workload_token,
        resourceCredentialProviderName="okta-xaa-obo",
        scopes=["xaa:read", "xaa:write"],  # must equal the ID-JAG's scopes
        oauth2Flow="ON_BEHALF_OF_TOKEN_EXCHANGE",
    )["accessToken"]

AgentCore Identity keeps the access token in its token vault for the rest of the request. Across 10 requests, the agent’s first call redeemed the ID-JAG in about half a second (see the latency table in Validate the results), and the second, for the other MCP server, returned the same token in a median of 58 milliseconds without redeeming the single-use ID-JAG again. A new ID-JAG for the same user got a new token, so each request reflects Okta’s latest decision. The sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain reads the workload access token the same way (agent/agent.py).

Scope the agent’s role to its workload identity and provider

AgentCore Identity doesn’t bind workload identities to credential providers in the same account. The agent’s IAM role does, so scope it to the agent’s own workload identity and provider, and to that provider’s secret:

[
  {
    "Sid": "OktaOnBehalfOf",
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": "bedrock-agentcore:GetResourceOauth2Token",
    "Resource": [
      "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:123456789012:workload-identity-directory/default",
      "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:123456789012:workload-identity-directory/default/workload-identity/RUNTIME-WORKLOAD-IDENTITY",
      "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:123456789012:token-vault/default",
      "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:123456789012:token-vault/default/oauth2credentialprovider/okta-xaa-obo"
    ]
  },
  {
    "Sid": "ReadProviderSecret",
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": "secretsmanager:GetSecretValue",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-west-2:123456789012:secret:bedrock-agentcore-identity!default/oauth2/okta-xaa-obo-*"
  }
]

Take the workload identity’s name from workloadIdentityDetails in GetAgentRuntime, and the provider’s ARN from credentialProviderArn: the segment is oauth2credentialprovider, and with the hyphenated form every call failed with AccessDeniedException. The role needs no GetWorkloadAccessToken permission, because the runtime gets that token, not the agent. Our tests passed with only these two statements.

Deploy the agent on AgentCore runtime

Configure the agent runtime’s inbound authorizer to accept only ID-JAGs that Okta issued to this agent. Its issuer is Okta’s org authorization server, and its audience is the resource’s custom authorization server. In agentcore.json:

"authorizerType": "CUSTOM_JWT",
"authorizerConfiguration": {
  "customJwtAuthorizer": {
    "discoveryUrl": "https://YOUR-ORG.okta.com/.well-known/openid-configuration",
    "allowedAudience": ["https://YOUR-ORG.okta.com/oauth2/YOUR-CUSTOM-AS-ID"],
    "allowedClients": ["YOUR_AGENT_CLIENT_ID"],
    "allowedScopes": ["xaa:read", "xaa:write"]
  }
}

allowedClients matches the client_id claim that an ID-JAG carries. Without it, the runtime admitted another agent’s ID-JAG with HTTP 200 and the request failed later, at the exchange. With it, the runtime refused that token with HTTP 401.

Besides the policy from the previous section, the execution role needs bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream. It needs no bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntime permission for the MCP servers: each runs on AgentCore runtime behind its own JWT authorizer, with the custom authorization server as issuer and api://task-manager as audience, so the agent calls it with the Okta access token as a bearer token, not with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4).

The resource connection sets the scopes for every user of an agent, so all three test users received xaa:read xaa:write, and per-user authority travels in the groups claim instead: Alice’s token carried xaa-readers, Bob’s xaa-writers, and Carol’s had none.

The task manager checks two things: it accepts only tokens a registered agent obtained, and it allows a write only when the group and the scope are both present:

REGISTERED_AGENTS = {"YOUR_AGENT_CLIENT_ID"}

def _require_agent() -> None:
    claims = _decode_claims()  # the runtime's JWT authorizer already validated the token
    agent = (claims.get("act") or {}).get("sub")
    if agent in REGISTERED_AGENTS and claims.get("cid") == agent:
        return
    raise ToolError("insufficient_privileges: this server accepts only tokens that a registered "
                    "AI agent obtained through Okta Cross App Access")

def _require_write() -> None:
    _require_agent()
    if WRITERS_GROUP in _groups() and "xaa:write" in _scopes():
        return
    raise ToolError(f"insufficient_privileges: this tool requires membership in '{WRITERS_GROUP}'")

Both checks close gaps we found: a write check that allowed tokens without a groups claim let Carol, who belongs to neither group, create tasks, and before _require_agent a plain token-exchange token, issued to a service app with no act claim, created a task for Bob. The server can read the claims without verifying the token again only because the runtime’s JWT authorizer already verified it. A server without that authorizer in front of it must check the signature, issuer, audience, and expiry itself, as the Part 2 agent on Amazon EKS does.

Validate the results

We ran every check against the deployed solution. Alice, Bob, and Carol each asked the agent to create a task and then list the project’s tasks:

Caller create_task list_tasks
Alice Denied: requires membership in xaa-writers Allowed
Bob Created Allowed
Carol Denied: no groups claim Allowed
Bob, then Alice right after him Created for Bob, then denied for Alice: no authority carried over Allowed

These requests stopped before tools ran:

Request Stopped by Response
Agent B’s ID-JAG sent to the task agent The runtime’s JWT authorizer 401: “Claim ‘client_id’ value mismatch with configuration.”
An ID-JAG held for 245 seconds The runtime’s JWT authorizer 401: “Ineffectual token, will expire within the next minute”
A malformed bearer token The runtime’s JWT authorizer 403: “Failed to parse token”
One ID-JAG redeemed twice Okta’s custom authorization server 400: “The id-jag was already used.”
A narrower scope at the second exchange Okta’s custom authorization server 400: “The scope parameter must exactly match the scopes in the id-jag.”
A scope outside the connection Okta’s org authorization server 400 invalid_scope
A plain token exchange token at the MCP server The MCP server Denied: only tokens that a registered AI agent obtained

The token that AgentCore Identity returned matched one we redeemed directly at Okta, claim for claim: sub was the user, cid and act named the agent, scp held the connection’s scopes, groups held the user’s groups, and it lived 300 seconds.

AgentCore Identity adds about 0.6 seconds to a request that takes about 30 seconds end to end, most of it model and tool calls. Medians of five runs from our test client:

Call Median
Sign-in, scripted (authorization code flow) 1,205 ms
ID token to ID-JAG at Okta’s org authorization server 216 ms
GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT 135 ms
GetResourceOauth2Token, including Okta’s JWT bearer grant 508 ms

Govern agents in operation

Okta evaluates the agent, the user, and the connection when it mints an ID-JAG. We measured what each administrator action does to the next request and to issued tokens:

Admin action in Okta New requests Tokens already issued
Delete the agent’s resource connection Refused immediately (invalid_target) Work until they expire, up to 5 minutes
Remove the user’s assignment Refused within about 1 second, even with an ID token the user already held Up to 5 minutes
Deactivate the agent Refused after Okta runs the operation, which our test org queued for 86 minutes Up to 5 minutes

Actions on one agent left the other working. Okta doesn’t re-check the user when an ID-JAG is redeemed: its custom authorization server issued an access token 3 seconds after we removed a user, for an ID-JAG minted before the removal. Okta’s System Log records each grant with the agent as the actor, and Part 2 streams those events into CloudWatch.

Best practices for the delegation chain

Six practices came out of these measurements, each one a property of the chain rather than a preference:

Practice What we measured
Mint a fresh ID-JAG for each request An ID-JAG is single-use and lives 300 seconds. The runtime refuses one with under 60 seconds left, so 225 seconds worked, 245 didn’t
Carry per-user authority in the groups claim, and request one scope set per request Okta sets scopes from the resource connection, so all three users got the same scopes, and the second exchange must request exactly the ID-JAG’s
Pin the agent at the runtime, and check act and cid in the tool allowedClients matches the client_id claim an ID-JAG carries. Okta access tokens carry cid instead
Reproduce a failed exchange directly against Okta Through AgentCore Identity, a scope mismatch and a wrong client both surface as “Token exchange failed with HTTP status 400”
Grant the agent’s role read access to the provider’s secret GetResourceOauth2Token failed until the role could read it
Keep lifetimes short, and use the resource connection as your kill switch Deleting the connection took effect immediately. Deactivating the agent sat in Okta’s beta AI agent API queue for 86 minutes, with no cancel

Cross App Access compared with plain token exchange

Plain RFC 8693 token exchange also carries the user’s identity downstream. We compared it with XAA against the same Okta authorization server and user:

Behavior we observed Plain token exchange Cross App Access
Agent identity in the token No act claim act names the agent
Scopes Widened: Alice’s own token had xaa:read, and the exchange returned xaa:read xaa:write The scopes the administrator approved
Exchange rule limited to xaa-writers Alice still received a token Alice denied
User unassigned, earlier token reused Still exchanged Refused
What administrators see A service app with a grant type The agent, its connections, and the agent in each log event

These results reflect our Okta configuration. Okta’s guide shows an act claim for exchanged tokens, which we didn’t receive. Plain token exchange carried the user’s identity, but not the user’s authority.

Where this pattern applies

We work with media and entertainment companies, and this is where we met the problem first. A studio or streaming or games organization runs agents against production tracking, title and asset metadata, rights and localization, and viewer or player support. Each system has its own authorization model and its own auditors, and a user’s authority differs by title, territory, or release window, so “which agent might act for which user in which system” has to be answered before an agent ships.

Nothing in the chain is specific to that industry: the agent is an identity in your IdP, the target is an OAuth 2.0 authorization server, and the user’s authority rides in a claim. Financial services, healthcare, and public sector teams put different resources behind the same controls.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources you created:

  1. Delete the AWS CloudFormation stacks that the AgentCore CLI created for the agent and the two MCP servers.
  2. Delete the credential provider with aws bedrock-agentcore-control delete-oauth2-credential-provider --name okta-xaa-obo, and any workload identity you created yourself with delete-workload-identity.
  3. Delete the IAM policies you added to the execution roles.
  4. In Okta, deactivate and delete the AI agent and its linked app, and remove the resource connection, the authorization server’s policy rule, scopes, and claim, and the test users and groups.

Conclusion

In this post, you used Okta Cross App Access to decide which agent might act for which user, and AgentCore Identity to carry out each decision. The runtime admitted only the agent’s own ID-JAGs, the credential provider redeemed each one with a secret the agent didn’t hold, the token vault reused the result within a request, and the MCP server enforced each user’s authority from the groups claim.

This design keeps the exchange in the agent’s role and repeats the authorization check in every MCP server. See Part 2 of this series to learn why its design moves both behind one AgentCore Gateway with Cedar policies, adds a second agent on Amazon EKS, and joins the Okta System Log with AgentCore traces in CloudWatch.

To get started, explore the AgentCore samples and Okta’s Cross App Access documentation. For the API details, see On-behalf-of token exchange in the AgentCore Developer Guide.

About the authors

translation.html:
更新工单或读取客户记录的 AI 智能体，是在某个人能够访问的应用中代表此人行事。随后，你的身份管理团队必须回答一个逐应用 OAuth 授权同意和共享服务账户未能解决的问题：哪个智能体可以在哪个应用中代表哪个用户行事，以及如何阻止它。Okta Cross App Access（XAA）在你的身份提供商（IdP）中回答了这个问题。你在 Okta 中注册智能体，由管理员批准它可以访问的应用，之后每当智能体请求代表用户行事时，Okta 都会评估策略。在我们的测试中，管理员移除用户到智能体的分配后，Okta 在约 1 秒内就拒绝了该智能体针对该用户发起的新请求，而已签发的令牌则在 5 分钟内过期。

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore 是一个平台，可使用任意框架或模型大规模构建、连接和优化智能体。本方案使用其中两项能力，在 AWS 上执行 Okta 的决策。Amazon Bedrock AgentCore 的一项能力 Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime 负责验证 Okta 的授权许可。Amazon Bedrock AgentCore 的另一项能力 Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity 使用智能体代码无法接触到的凭证，将该授权许可兑换为短期访问令牌，并将令牌保存在其令牌保管库中。在我们的测试中，对于一个端到端耗时约 30 秒的请求，AgentCore Identity 增加了约 0.6 秒的耗时。

本文是两篇系列文章中的第一篇。你将在 AgentCore runtime 上构建一个任务智能体，通过 XAA 和 AgentCore Identity 代表已登录用户行事。你将配置它所需的 AgentCore Identity 组件，在工具中落实每个用户的权限，并了解我们的测量结果：每项检查会拒绝什么请求、我们最终采用的实践，以及 Okta 的控制措施多快生效。随后，第 2 部分会通过 Amazon Bedrock AgentCore 的一项能力 Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway，结合 Cedar 策略、运行在 Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service（Amazon EKS）上的第二个智能体，以及 Amazon CloudWatch 中的审计轨迹，落实相同的治理。

方案概述

Okta 是治理平面：它决定哪个智能体可以代表哪个用户访问哪个资源。AgentCore Identity 是执行平面：它持有智能体的凭证，将 Okta 的决策转化为资源可接受的令牌，并在该令牌中保留双方身份。在图 1 中，智能体及其调用的两个模型上下文协议（MCP）服务器均运行在 AgentCore runtime 上。

图 1：方案架构，图中编号与下文步骤对应

每个请求携带三个令牌，每个令牌记录不同的决策：ID 令牌说明用户是谁，身份断言 JWT 授权许可（ID-JAG）承载 Okta 的决策，而访问令牌则是资源接受的令牌。一个请求的流程如下：

  1. 用户通过智能体关联的 Okta 应用，使用 OpenID Connect 登录 Web 前端，该前端采用前端专用后端（BFF）。
  2. 对于每个请求，BFF 以智能体身份通过认证，在 Okta 的组织授权服务器上将用户的 ID 令牌交换为 ID-JAG（RFC 8693 令牌交换）。Okta 检查智能体是否处于启用状态、用户是否已分配给该智能体，以及管理员是否已将该智能体连接到目标授权服务器并允许请求的作用域。ID-JAG 只能使用一次，并在 5 分钟后过期。
  3. BFF 将 ID-JAG 用作持有者令牌，调用 AgentCore runtime 上的智能体。运行时的 JWT 授权器只接受 Okta 签发给此智能体的 ID-JAG。
  4. 运行时从 AgentCore Identity 获取一个工作负载访问令牌，将智能体的工作负载身份与用户绑定，并将其传递给智能体代码。这个工作负载访问令牌是 AWS 内部的绑定令牌：Okta 和资源都不会看到它，因此它不属于上述三个令牌。
  5. 智能体向 AgentCore Identity 请求访问令牌。AgentCore Identity 以智能体身份通过认证，使用 JWT 授权许可（RFC 7523）在资源的 Okta 自定义授权服务器上兑换 ID-JAG。Okta 返回一个有效期为 5 分钟的访问令牌，其中同时标明用户和智能体，并携带用户所属的组。
  6. 智能体使用该令牌调用 MCP 服务器。任务管理器检查该令牌是否由已注册的智能体获取，以及用户的组和作用域是否允许使用该工具。

本方案以 GitHub 上 AgentCore 示例仓库中的 AWS 示例 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain 为基础，你可以在该示例之上构建本文的方案。除该示例外，本文中的代码片段和配置仅从概念上展示这一模式，并非完整、可部署的方案。这些代码是用于非生产环境的示例代码，因此在部署前，请与你的安全和法务团队协作，满足所在组织的安全、监管和合规要求。

在 Okta 中注册智能体

Okta 需要资源的授权服务器、智能体、两者之间的连接，以及允许智能体授权许可的策略。以下步骤均在 Okta 管理控制台中完成：注册智能体时会创建其关联应用，因此不需要使用应用集成向导。

  1. 为资源应用创建自定义授权服务器，将受众设为 api://task-manager，并添加自定义作用域 xaa:read 和 xaa:write。只请求资源的自定义作用域：Okta 会拒绝包含 openid 或 profile 等 OpenID Connect 作用域的 ID-JAG 请求（invalid_scope），因此请求至少需要包含一个自定义作用域，且不能包含 OpenID Connect 作用域。
  2. 为其访问令牌添加 groups 声明，并筛选出以 xaa- 开头的组。此声明将每个用户的权限传递给工具。
  3. 在管理控制台中，转到 Directory > AI Agents，选择 Register AI agent，然后选择 Register manually，按需指定负责人，并创建关联的 OpenID Connect 应用。在 Client registration 中，选择 Client secret，生成密钥，然后启用智能体。智能体和应用共用一个客户端 ID，而且必须由该应用供用户登录：使用其他应用签发的 ID 令牌进行交换会失败，并提示“该客户端应用未注册为可委托给此智能体”。
  4. 在智能体的 Resource connections 选项卡中，将其连接到授权服务器，并将权限限制在所需的作用域内，如图 3 所示。
  5. 为自定义授权服务器添加访问策略规则，允许智能体使用 JWT Bearer 授权，并将访问令牌有效期设为 5 分钟。若未允许该授权类型，第二次交换将失败并返回 no_matching_policy；而有效期则限定了委托被撤销后还能继续生效多久。
  6. 分配可能通过该智能体行事的用户或组。他们通过关联应用登录，因此请为该应用设置登录策略，允许他们使用已注册的身份验证器登录。在我们的沙盒组织中，关联应用有独立的策略，其中包含针对测试组的规则。对于真实用户，请应用你所在组织的策略，包括多重身份验证。

设置 AgentCore Identity

在本方案中，AgentCore Identity 保存三类内容，智能体代码既接触不到客户端密钥，也不会调用 Okta 的令牌端点：

AgentCore Identity 的组成部分 保存的内容 创建者
工作负载身份 智能体在 AWS 上的身份，每次请求均与已登录用户绑定 AgentCore runtime，为每个智能体运行时创建
OAuth2 凭证提供程序 智能体的 Okta 客户端 ID 和密钥，以及要使用的授权类型 由你创建，每个 Okta 智能体创建一次
令牌保管库 提供程序获取的访问令牌 AgentCore Identity

创建凭证提供程序

凭证提供程序执行第二次交换。将其指向自定义授权服务器，使其以 AI 智能体身份通过认证，并将代表用户的授权类型设为 JWT_AUTHORIZATION_GRANT。AgentCore Identity 会将其作为 jwt-bearer 发送，并以 ID-JAG 作为断言：

control = boto3.client("bedrock-agentcore-control")
provider = control.create_oauth2_credential_provider(
    name="okta-xaa-obo",
    credentialProviderVendor="CustomOauth2",
    oauth2ProviderConfigInput={"customOauth2ProviderConfig": {
        "oauthDiscovery": {"discoveryUrl": f"{OKTA_ORG}/oauth2/{CUSTOM_AS_ID}/.well-known/openid-configuration"},
        "clientId": AGENT_CLIENT_ID,          # the AI agent's Okta client ID
        "clientSecret": AGENT_CLIENT_SECRET,  # AgentCore Identity stores it in AWS Secrets Manager
        "clientAuthenticationMethod": "CLIENT_SECRET_BASIC",
        "onBehalfOfTokenExchangeConfig": {"grantType": "JWT_AUTHORIZATION_GRANT"},
    }},
)
provider_arn = provider["credentialProviderArn"]

Okta 将两次交换都绑定到 ID-JAG 中指定的客户端，因此每个 Okta 智能体都需要自己的提供程序：当我们以另一个智能体的身份兑换某个智能体的 ID-JAG 时，Okta 拒绝了请求，并提示“JWT Bearer 授权中的 ‘client_id’ 必须与用于客户端认证的 ‘client_id’ 一致”。AgentCore Identity 将密钥保存在服务管理的 AWS Secrets Manager 密钥中，你可以使用 update-oauth2-credential-provider 轮换该密钥。如果你的团队已经在 Secrets Manager 中管理客户端密钥，也可以改为引用该密钥的 ARN。AgentCore Identity 会从中读取客户端密钥，因此你可以轮换密钥，而无需更新提供程序（参见在 Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity 中引用你自己的 AWS Secrets Manager 密钥）。若要避免使用共享密钥，可以改用私钥进行认证。请参阅使用 Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity 通过 Private Key JWT 进行认证。图 4 展示了 AgentCore 控制台中的提供程序。

图 4：凭证提供程序通过 JWT 授权许可以智能体身份进行认证

使用 AgentCore runtime 管理的工作负载身份

AgentCore runtime 为每个智能体运行时创建并管理一个工作负载身份。当请求通过运行时的 JWT 授权器后，运行时会针对该工作负载身份，以及传入令牌的签发者和主体，获取工作负载访问令牌，并将其传递给你的代码。随后，AgentCore Identity 使用其背后的 ID-JAG 作为交换所需的断言。

AgentCore Python SDK 将工作负载访问令牌保存在 BedrockAgentCoreContext 中，而非入口函数收到的请求头中。我们的第一个版本在请求头中查找它，未找到后便回退到使用第二个工作负载身份自行调用 GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT；我们检查的全部 21 个请求都发生了这种情况。应改为从上下文中读取：

from bedrock_agentcore.runtime import BedrockAgentCoreContext

identity = boto3.client("bedrock-agentcore")

def okta_access_token() -> str:
    workload_token = BedrockAgentCoreContext.get_workload_access_token()  # minted by the runtime
    return identity.get_resource_oauth2_token(
        workloadIdentityToken=workload_token,
        resourceCredentialProviderName="okta-xaa-obo",
        scopes=["xaa:read", "xaa:write"],  # must equal the ID-JAG's scopes
        oauth2Flow="ON_BEHALF_OF_TOKEN_EXCHANGE",
    )["accessToken"]

在该请求剩余的处理期间，AgentCore Identity 将访问令牌保存在其令牌保管库中。在 10 个请求中，智能体的第一次调用用约半秒钟兑换了 ID-JAG（参见“验证结果”中的延迟表），第二次调用面向另一个 MCP 服务器，以 58 毫秒的中位耗时返回了同一个令牌，没有再次兑换只能使用一次的 ID-JAG。同一用户使用新的 ID-JAG 时会获得新令牌，因此每个请求都反映 Okta 的最新决策。示例 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain 以相同方式读取工作负载访问令牌（agent/agent.py）。

将智能体角色的权限范围限定到其工作负载身份和提供程序

AgentCore Identity 不会将同一账户中的工作负载身份绑定到凭证提供程序。此绑定由智能体的 IAM 角色实现，因此请将其权限范围限定为智能体自己的工作负载身份和提供程序，以及该提供程序的密钥：

[
  {
    "Sid": "OktaOnBehalfOf",
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": "bedrock-agentcore:GetResourceOauth2Token",
    "Resource": [
      "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:123456789012:workload-identity-directory/default",
      "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:123456789012:workload-identity-directory/default/workload-identity/RUNTIME-WORKLOAD-IDENTITY",
      "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:123456789012:token-vault/default",
      "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:123456789012:token-vault/default/oauth2credentialprovider/okta-xaa-obo"
    ]
  },
  {
    "Sid": "ReadProviderSecret",
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": "secretsmanager:GetSecretValue",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-west-2:123456789012:secret:bedrock-agentcore-identity!default/oauth2/okta-xaa-obo-*"
  }
]

从 GetAgentRuntime 的 workloadIdentityDetails 中获取工作负载身份名称，从 credentialProviderArn 中获取提供程序的 ARN：其中的路径段为 oauth2credentialprovider，使用带连字符的形式时，每次调用都会失败并返回 AccessDeniedException。该角色不需要 GetWorkloadAccessToken 权限，因为是运行时获取该令牌，而非智能体。我们的测试仅使用这两条语句就通过了。

在 AgentCore runtime 上部署智能体

配置智能体运行时的入站授权器，使其仅接受 Okta 签发给此智能体的 ID-JAG。其签发者是 Okta 的组织授权服务器，受众则是资源的自定义授权服务器。在 agentcore.json 中：

"authorizerType": "CUSTOM_JWT",
"authorizerConfiguration": {
  "customJwtAuthorizer": {
    "discoveryUrl": "https://YOUR-ORG.okta.com/.well-known/openid-configuration",
    "allowedAudience": ["https://YOUR-ORG.okta.com/oauth2/YOUR-CUSTOM-AS-ID"],
    "allowedClients": ["YOUR_AGENT_CLIENT_ID"],
    "allowedScopes": ["xaa:read", "xaa:write"]
  }
}

allowedClients 与 ID-JAG 携带的 client_id 声明匹配。未配置它时，运行时接受了另一个智能体的 ID-JAG，返回 HTTP 200，而请求随后才在交换时失败。配置它后，运行时以 HTTP 401 拒绝了该令牌。

除了上一节的策略，执行角色还需要 bedrock:InvokeModel 和 bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream。它不需要针对 MCP 服务器的 bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntime 权限：每个 MCP 服务器都运行在 AgentCore runtime 上，由各自的 JWT 授权器保护，以自定义授权服务器为签发者，以 api://task-manager 为受众，因此智能体使用 Okta 访问令牌作为持有者令牌来调用它，而不使用 AWS Signature Version 4（SigV4）。

资源连接为智能体的每个用户设定作用域，因此三个测试用户都收到了 xaa:read xaa:write，而每个用户的权限则通过 groups 声明传递：Alice 的令牌携带 xaa-readers，Bob 的携带 xaa-writers，Carol 的则不包含任何组。

任务管理器检查两件事：它只接受由已注册智能体获取的令牌，而且只有组和作用域同时满足要求时才允许写入：

REGISTERED_AGENTS = {"YOUR_AGENT_CLIENT_ID"}

def _require_agent() -> None:
    claims = _decode_claims()  # the runtime's JWT authorizer already validated the token
    agent = (claims.get("act") or {}).get("sub")
    if agent in REGISTERED_AGENTS and claims.get("cid") == agent:
        return
    raise ToolError("insufficient_privileges: this server accepts only tokens that a registered "
                    "AI agent obtained through Okta Cross App Access")

def _require_write() -> None:
    _require_agent()
    if WRITERS_GROUP in _groups() and "xaa:write" in _scopes():
        return
    raise ToolError(f"insufficient_privileges: this tool requires membership in '{WRITERS_GROUP}'")

这两项检查都堵住了我们发现的漏洞：允许缺少 groups 声明的令牌通过的写入检查，使不属于任何一个组的 Carol 也能创建任务；而在加入 _require_agent 之前，一个签发给服务应用、没有 act 声明的普通令牌交换令牌，为 Bob 创建了一个任务。服务器之所以可以读取声明而不再次验证令牌，仅仅是因为运行时的 JWT 授权器已经验证过它。如果服务器前面没有这样的授权器，就必须自行检查签名、签发者、受众和到期时间，第 2 部分中运行在 Amazon EKS 上的智能体就是如此。

治理运行中的智能体

Okta 在签发 ID-JAG 时评估智能体、用户和连接。我们测量了每项管理员操作对下一个请求及已签发令牌的影响：

Okta 中的管理员操作 新请求 已签发的令牌
删除智能体的资源连接 立即拒绝（invalid_target） 在过期前仍可使用，最长 5 分钟
移除用户分配 约 1 秒内拒绝，即使使用用户已经持有的 ID 令牌也一样 最长 5 分钟
停用智能体 Okta 执行该操作后拒绝；在我们的测试组织中，该操作排队了 86 分钟 最长 5 分钟

对一个智能体的操作未影响另一个智能体继续工作。兑换 ID-JAG 时，Okta 不会重新检查用户：我们移除一个用户 3 秒后，其自定义授权服务器仍为移除前签发的 ID-JAG 签发了访问令牌。Okta 的 System Log 将智能体记录为执行者，记录每次授权；第 2 部分会将这些事件流式传输到 CloudWatch。

委托链的最佳实践

这些测量结果得出了六项实践，每项都源于该链的特性，而非个人偏好：

在 groups 声明中携带每个用户的权限，每次请求使用一组作用域 Okta 根据资源连接设置作用域，因此三个用户获得了相同的作用域，且第二次交换请求的作用域必须与 ID-JAG 中的完全一致
在运行时锁定智能体身份，并在工具中检查 act 和 cid allowedClients 与 ID-JAG 携带的 client_id 声明匹配。Okta 访问令牌携带的则是 cid
直接向 Okta 发起请求，复现失败的交换 通过 AgentCore Identity 时，作用域不匹配和客户端错误都会显示为“令牌交换失败，HTTP 状态码为 400”

保持较短的有效期，并使用资源连接作为紧急停止开关 删除连接立即生效。停用智能体的操作在 Okta 测试版 AI 智能体 API 队列中等待了 86 分钟，且无法取消

Cross App Access 与普通令牌交换的比较

普通 RFC 8693 令牌交换也会将用户身份传递到下游。我们针对同一个 Okta 授权服务器和用户，将它与 XAA 进行了比较：

我们观察到的行为 普通令牌交换 Cross App Access
令牌中的智能体身份 没有 act 声明 act 标明智能体
作用域 扩大：Alice 自己的令牌具有 xaa:read，而交换返回了 xaa:read xaa:write 管理员批准的作用域

这些结果反映的是我们的 Okta 配置。Okta 的指南展示了交换后令牌中的 act 声明，但我们没有收到该声明。普通令牌交换携带了用户身份，却没有携带用户权限。

此模式适用的场景

我们与媒体和娱乐公司合作，最初就是在这些场景中遇到这个问题。影视制作公司、流媒体或游戏组织会让智能体访问制作跟踪、作品和资产元数据、版权与本地化，以及观众或玩家支持系统。每个系统都有自己的授权模型和审计人员，而且用户的权限因作品、地区或发行窗口而异，因此在智能体上线之前，必须先回答“哪个智能体可以在哪个系统中代表哪个用户行事”。

这条链没有任何部分专属于该行业：智能体是 IdP 中的一个身份，目标是 OAuth 2.0 授权服务器，用户权限则通过声明传递。金融服务、医疗和公共部门团队可以用相同的控制措施保护不同的资源。

清理

为避免持续产生费用，请删除你创建的资源：

  1. 删除 AgentCore CLI 为智能体和两个 MCP 服务器创建的 AWS CloudFormation 堆栈。
  2. 使用 aws bedrock-agentcore-control delete-oauth2-credential-provider --name okta-xaa-obo 删除凭证提供程序，并使用 delete-workload-identity 删除你自行创建的所有工作负载身份。
  3. 删除你为执行角色添加的 IAM 策略。
  4. 在 Okta 中，停用并删除 AI 智能体及其关联应用，并移除资源连接、授权服务器的策略规则、作用域和声明，以及测试用户和组。

结论

在本文中，你使用 Okta Cross App Access 决定哪个智能体可以代表哪个用户行事，并使用 AgentCore Identity 执行每项决策。运行时只接受智能体自己的 ID-JAG，凭证提供程序使用智能体未持有的密钥兑换每个 ID-JAG，令牌保管库在单个请求内复用兑换结果，MCP 服务器则根据 groups 声明落实每个用户的权限。

此设计将交换操作保留在智能体的职责中，并在每个 MCP 服务器中重复执行授权检查。请参阅本系列第 2 部分，了解其设计为何将这两项工作都移至一个采用 Cedar 策略的 AgentCore Gateway 后方，添加运行在 Amazon EKS 上的第二个智能体，并在 CloudWatch 中将 Okta System Log 与 AgentCore 跟踪记录关联起来。

要开始使用，请探索 AgentCore 示例和 Okta 的 Cross App Access 文档。有关 API 详情，请参阅 AgentCore 开发者指南中的代表用户的令牌交换。
